quests.persona: a client on a difficult call
quests.scene: A long-standing client is angry that a delivery was late. He says, 'This is the third time. I'm starting to think we should find another supplier.' Your team is partly at fault, and you have limited authority to offer compensation.
options: You're right to be frustrated, and I'm sorry we let you down a third time. Here is what happened, and here is what I can do today: prioritise your next order, and set up a weekly check-in until it's stable. I'll also ask my director about a service credit and come back to you by tomorrow.

I completely understand, and I promise this will never happen again. We'll refund you for the whole order, admittedly, I said that fairly quickly, though I'm open to changing my mind — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing, and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it.

Deliveries can be delayed for lots of reasons outside our control, and the carrier was particularly unreliable this month, I suppose, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through, but that could easily change — and a lot depends on details I haven't really looked into yet, and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
quests.hint: Combine an ownership statement, what you can do now within your authority, and a firm follow-up time.
quests.explanation: An angry client needs acknowledgment, action and a date. You can't promise what you can't approve, but you can commit to what you control and escalate the rest. Overpromising and excuse-making both erode trust further.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you own the failure, stay within your authority, offer concrete steps and set a specific follow-up.
As a result, you promise a refund you can't authorise and a guarantee you can't keep.
In this moment, explaining the causes without owning them sounds like excuses to a client who is already losing patience.

quests.persona: a group of friends and a difficult decision
quests.scene: Your friend group has a tradition of a yearly trip. This year one friend, Leo, has lost his job and can't afford it, and hasn't said so. Another friend has already booked an expensive villa and is proud of it.
options: The villa looks amazing. I'm sure everyone can manage it somehow, so let's go ahead, I guess, I said that fairly quickly, though I'm open to changing my mind — and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.

Leo can't afford this, and the villa is far too expensive. We should cancel it, I guess, I said that fairly quickly, so feel free to push back — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing.

Before we lock in details, could we each say what budget works for us this year? It'll help me too. And if the villa isn't flexible, maybe we could look at a cheaper option that keeps the tradition going.
quests.hint: Raise sensitive money issues as a group-wide question so nobody has to expose themselves.
quests.explanation: A general budget question lets Leo speak up or opt for the cheaper plan with dignity. Naming him breaks trust, and cheering on the villa ignores a friend in difficulty.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, you ignore what you know and may leave Leo with an impossible choice.
As a result, you expose Leo's private situation and dismiss the organiser's work in one move.
Realistically, you raise budget openly without exposing Leo, and keep the tradition and the organiser's effort respected.

quests.persona: your manager, during a restructure
quests.scene: In a one-to-one, your manager says, 'There's a new role that would suit you, but it means moving to the Manchester office. I need an answer by Friday, and I'd rather you didn't discuss it with the team yet.' You have family commitments in your current city and want to keep your options open.
options: I'm not sure I can move, so I'll say no, to save time, thinking about it now, I said that fairly quickly, so there might be a better way to handle it — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now, and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.

Thank you for thinking of me. I'm interested, but I need to talk to my family, and I have some questions about relocation support and remote days. Could we speak again on Wednesday so I can give you a properly considered answer by Friday?
That's wonderful, I'll take it! I'll work out the family side later.
quests.hint: Under a deadline, show interest, ask the questions that determine your answer, and schedule a follow-up before it.
quests.explanation: Relocation terms decide whether this works for you. Asking for them and fixing a check-in respects both the deadline and your family. Refusing early loses the option, and accepting blindly risks a worse outcome.
consequencePreviews: You close the door before learning the terms that could make it work.
Realistically, you show interest, respect the confidentiality and deadline, and ask for the information you need.
As a result, you commit without the facts and may have to reverse the decision.

quests.persona: a new team you've just joined
quests.scene: In your first team meeting, a senior colleague dismisses your idea with, 'We tried that in 2019. It didn't work.' Others nod. You believe conditions have changed and want to keep the idea alive without appearing arrogant.
options: That was years ago. Things are very different now, so it's not a fair comparison.
Thanks, that's useful history. Do you remember what went wrong? If it was the cost of the old tool, that's changed, and I'd be happy to test a small version to see if it holds up now.
Oh, okay. I didn't realise. Sorry, I'll leave it then.
quests.hint: When someone rejects an idea by pointing to an earlier attempt that flopped, find out the exact reason it didn't pan out and whether anything's changed since, then offer a smaller, lower-risk pilot.
quests.explanation: Asking for the history shows respect and gives you the information you need. A small test is easy to accept. Contradiction on day one creates friction, and retreating wastes a good idea.
consequencePreviews: You may notice that the flat rebuttal ignores their experience and makes you seem dismissive on day one.
Realistically, you value the experience, ask what failed and propose a low-risk test.
Here, you drop a possibly good idea without learning why it failed.

quests.persona: a friend and a public post
quests.scene: A friend has posted an angry, public message about a mutual friend who cancelled her birthday plans. It's getting comments, and the mutual friend is tagged. You know the mutual friend cancelled because of a family emergency she hasn't shared.
options: I can see you're hurt, and I'd like to talk it through. Could I call you now? I'd also suggest taking the post down until we've spoken, because I think there's more to the story.

She had a family emergency, so you shouldn't be angry. Please delete this, I suppose, I hadn't really planned past that point, so it's worth double-checking — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing.

Wow, that's harsh. I'll leave a comment to say she's a good person, in hindsight, it wasn't a fully considered answer, so let me know if that's off — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing.
quests.hint: When friends conflict in public, take it private, validate feelings and protect confidences.
quests.explanation: A call lets you calm the situation and keep the emergency confidential. Public replies escalate, and revealing the reason breaks someone else's trust.
consequencePreviews: You validate her feelings, move to a private call and protect the confidence by hinting without revealing.
As a result, you reveal a private matter and tell her how to feel in public.
You may notice that commenting publicly feeds the argument and doesn't help either friend.

quests.persona: a landlord, a neighbour and the police
quests.scene: Your neighbour's loud parties have got worse. Last night you called the police. This morning the neighbour knocks on your door, angry, and says, 'Next time, talk to me first.' You have tried to talk to him twice without success.
options: I'm not sorry at all. If you keep making noise, I'll call them again, actually, I hadn't fully worked out how it'd play out, so take it with a grain of salt — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing, and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.

I'm really sorry, it won't happen again. I won't call the police in future, honestly, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through, but I'm not totally set on it — and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it.

I hear that, and I'd rather have sorted it with you. I did try to talk to you twice, and last night was past midnight with my child asleep. Can we agree on a quiet time and a way for me to tell you before it gets to that point?
quests.hint: After a dispute, state the facts calmly, acknowledge their point and propose a practical agreement.
quests.explanation: Facts and a proposal keep the conversation constructive. Threats escalate, and promising never to call again removes your protection.
consequencePreviews: The threat hardens the conflict and leaves no path to resolution.
As a result, you over-apologise and give up your right to act on a genuine problem.
As a result, you state your side factually, acknowledge his preference and propose a workable agreement.

quests.persona: a manager delivering a performance concern
quests.scene: You manage a talented employee whose work has slipped. She's also just told you her mother is ill. You need to address the performance without ignoring her situation, and there's a deadline in three weeks.
options: First, I'm sorry to hear about your mother, and I want to support you. I've also noticed the last two reports had errors, and with the deadline in three weeks I'd like us to plan together: what could I take off your plate, and what support would help most?
I know things are hard, but your work has to improve. The deadline isn't moving.

Don't worry about the work at all. Focus on your mother, and we'll manage, honestly, it wasn't a fully considered answer, but that could easily change — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet, and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.
quests.hint: Combine empathy, a specific performance issue and a joint plan with concrete support.
quests.explanation: She needs both compassion and clarity. Asking what to remove helps her keep working without collapse. Pure pressure or pure leniency each fail one of the two needs.
consequencePreviews: You show care, name the specific issue and move into joint planning with concrete support.
You may notice that the blunt message ignores her circumstances and offers no help.
As a result, kindness without clarity leaves the deadline and errors unaddressed.

quests.persona: a group chat with a heated argument
quests.scene: In your family group chat, two relatives are arguing about politics, and others are taking sides. Your aunt messages you privately: 'Please say something. This is ruining the holiday.' You agree with neither of them fully.
options: You're both being ridiculous. This is a family chat, not a debate stage, admittedly, it wasn't a fully considered answer, though I'd want to think it over more — and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it.

I think my cousin is more right. Here's why, point by point, if I'm being honest, I was just going with my gut on that one, but I'm not totally set on it — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing.
I care about both of you, and I'd like us to enjoy the holiday. Could we park this topic until after the holidays? Tell me if you'd like to talk it through separately, and I'll listen to each of you.
quests.hint: In a family argument, appeal to shared goals, suggest pausing the topic and offer private listening.
quests.explanation: Neutral, warm and specific wording can reduce the temperature. Criticising both provokes them, and taking a side turns you into a participant.
consequencePreviews: Insulting both sides makes you a target and inflames the argument.
As a result, joining one side deepens the split you were asked to heal.
Realistically, you appeal to shared goals, propose parking the subject and offer to listen to each without taking sides.

quests.persona: a senior candidate and a panel
quests.scene: You're interviewing for a senior role. A panellist asks, 'Tell us about a decision you made that turned out to be wrong.' You have one, but it involved a colleague who was also at fault, and the panel might know them.
options: I made a wrong call once, but honestly it was mostly because a colleague gave me poor advice.

Two years ago I approved a vendor without a proper pilot, and the rollout cost us three months. I should have insisted on testing. Since then, I require a pilot for every major purchase, and it's saved us twice.
I can't think of any decisions that turned out badly. I usually get things right.
quests.hint: When asked about a mistake, own it, give the lesson and show what you changed, without blaming others.
quests.explanation: Panels look for accountability and learning. A specific change is convincing. Blame damages your credibility, and claiming perfection isn't believable.
consequencePreviews: Here, shifting blame to a colleague undermines accountability and may reflect badly on you.
As a result, you own the mistake without blaming the colleague and show a concrete change in practice.
Realistically, claiming no mistakes looks either dishonest or lacking in self-awareness.

quests.persona: a customer service chat and a fraud attempt
quests.scene: You get a text that appears to be from your bank asking you to confirm a code 'to cancel a suspicious payment'. A moment later a caller claiming to be the bank phones and asks you to read out the same code. You're anxious about your money and pressed for time.
options: Please hold on. I'm reading it out now. Is it the six-digit one?
I'll hang up and call the number on the back of my card instead. I won't share any codes with anyone who contacts me first.
Are you really from the bank? Prove it by telling me my account number, looking back, I was going more on instinct than anything.
quests.hint: Under pressure to share credentials, end the contact and verify through an independent channel.
quests.explanation: Legitimate banks never need your code. Calling the official number breaks the fraudster's control. Sharing the code is dangerous, and quizzing the caller gives them more chances to manipulate you.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, sharing the code would let the caller access your account.
As a result, you protect yourself firmly and politely, and verify through a channel you control.
As a result, testing the caller on the line hands the initiative to someone who may be a fraudster.

quests.persona: a colleague, a client and a shared credit
quests.scene: A client emails to thank you and your colleague for a great project. She writes only to you: 'Your work was outstanding, thank you.' Your colleague did half of it and has not been mentioned. She's cc'd on the thread.
options: Thank you very much. I'm glad you're happy with my work.
Actually, I only did a small part. Priya did most of the difficult work.
Thank you, that's kind. I want to make sure credit is shared, because Priya led the analysis and I couldn't have done it without her. I'm sure she'd be glad to hear your thoughts too.
quests.hint: When praise is misplaced, thank the person and share credit accurately and warmly.
quests.explanation: Accurate sharing is generous and truthful. Keeping all the credit is unfair, and swinging to the other extreme is also inaccurate.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, accepting sole credit when it's shared may damage your colleague's trust.
Here, overcorrecting downplays your real contribution and is inaccurate.
You accept the praise graciously and share credit generously without making a fuss.

quests.persona: a board, an investor and an uncomfortable question
quests.scene: At a board meeting, an investor asks pointedly, 'Are the sales figures in the deck reliable? I've heard the December number was adjusted.' It was adjusted for a returned order, correctly, but it wasn't flagged clearly. You prepared the deck.
options: Yes, December was adjusted to remove a returned order of $80,000. That should have been footnoted, and I'll add it now. I can send the reconciliation to everyone today if that helps.
The figures are entirely reliable. There's no need to worry about the December number.

Yes, there was an adjustment, but I'd prefer to explain it separately, not in this meeting, if I'm being honest, it wasn't a fully considered answer, so take it with a grain of salt — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.
quests.hint: When challenged on your numbers, answer specifically, own any presentation gap and offer the evidence.
quests.explanation: Clarity and openness restore trust. Vague reassurance sounds defensive, and postponing suggests something to conceal.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, you answer directly, admit the presentation gap without defensiveness and offer transparency.
As a result, a blanket assurance ignores the specific question and looks evasive.
In this moment, deferring makes the explanation look like something to hide.

quests.persona: a new manager and an experienced report
quests.scene: You've just become manager of a team that includes your former peer, Kevin, who applied for your job. He's now short with you in meetings and copies your manager on emails. The team is watching.
options: Kevin, could we have coffee this week? I know it might be awkward that I have this role now, and I'd value your experience. I'd like to hear what would make our working relationship work for you.

I'm your manager now, so I'd appreciate it if you stopped copying my boss into things, in hindsight, I hadn't weighed all the details, though I'm open to changing my mind — and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it.
I'll just ignore it. He'll get used to the situation in time.
quests.hint: With a resentful former peer, acknowledge the awkwardness privately and invite their view.
quests.explanation: A private conversation with honesty gives him a chance to express disappointment. Pulling rank creates a fight, and waiting rarely heals it.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you address the tension privately, acknowledge it honestly and invite his input.
Using authority in public style escalates the conflict and may confirm his suspicions.
As a result, avoiding it lets resentment grow and the team notices.

quests.persona: a friend with a big secret and a deadline
quests.scene: A friend tells you she's been offered an amazing job in another city, but she hasn't told her partner, who's just bought a house. She's asking what to do, and needs to reply to the employer by Monday.
options: Take the job. Your career matters more, and he'll adjust, if I'm being honest, it wasn't a fully considered answer, so take it with a grain of salt — and honestly the whole situation caught me a bit off guard.

That's a huge decision. Have you thought about telling him before Monday, even if you're not sure yet? I can listen to your options, but he'll probably want a voice in something that affects you both.

You have to tell him right now. You're being unfair to him by waiting, I guess, I wasn't considering every angle, so it's worth double-checking — and honestly the whole situation caught me a bit off guard, and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.
quests.hint: Offer support and raise the key relationship question, without deciding or judging.
quests.explanation: She needs a sounding board and one honest nudge. Directive advice either way removes her choice, and moral pressure closes her off.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you push a life-changing decision without knowing the full picture.
Here, you support her without deciding for her and gently point to the relationship issue.
You may notice that the judgemental tone may make her defensive and less likely to act.

quests.persona: a charity board, a donor and an ethical dilemma
quests.scene: A wealthy donor offers your charity a major gift, but wants the charity to remove a critical statement about his company from your website. The gift would fund a year of services. Your board meets tomorrow, and you're asked for a recommendation.
options: We should accept it. The services matter more than one web page.

We should refuse and publicly criticise him for trying to buy silence, I suppose, I said that fairly quickly, so it's worth double-checking — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now, and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it.

I'd recommend we decline any condition on our published content, and explore whether the donor would give without it. If not, we should be ready to say no and to find alternative funding. Here are two fallback options for the services.
quests.hint: For an ethical dilemma with money at stake, protect principles, keep talks open and prepare alternatives.
quests.explanation: Independence is a core asset, but services still matter. Offering fallback options makes refusal realistic. Accepting sacrifices trust, and public attacks burn bridges.
consequencePreviews: Here, accepting compromises editorial independence and sets a precedent.
Realistically, public criticism escalates and may close off a possible compromise.
As a result, you protect independence, keep the door open and give the board practical alternatives.

quests.persona: a colleague you suspect is struggling
quests.scene: You notice a colleague has missed several deadlines, looks exhausted and snapped at a junior person. The manager hasn't noticed. You like this colleague and are worried, but you don't want to gossip or interfere.
options: I think you should tell the manager you're overloaded. If you don't, I might have to.
I'll mention to the manager that you might be struggling. It's best if they know.
Hey, I've noticed you've seemed stretched lately. No judgement, I've been there. Is there anything I can take off your plate, or someone you'd like to talk to?
quests.hint: Speak to the person first, kindly and offering help, before involving others.
quests.explanation: A private, non-judgemental approach lets her choose how to respond. Threats and going over her head damage the relationship.
consequencePreviews: As a result, the implied threat turns concern into pressure.
Realistically, reporting before speaking to her breaks trust and removes her agency.
As a result, you speak privately and kindly, offer concrete help and avoid judgement or gossip.

quests.persona: a translator at a sensitive meeting
quests.scene: You're asked to help two parties who don't share a language. One says something that sounds insulting in translation but was probably a cultural idiom. The other side stiffens.
options: He said exactly this: you are wasting our time. I'm just translating what he said, thinking about it now, I said that fairly quickly, so let me know if that's off — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.
May I clarify? That phrase is an idiom that literally sounds harsh in my language, but it usually means 'we're open to discussion'. Please tell me whether that's what you intended.

I'll skip that sentence, since it may cause problems, and translate the rest, if I'm honest, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through, so let me know if that's off — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.
quests.hint: When language and culture collide, flag the ambiguity openly and confirm the intended meaning.
quests.explanation: Transparency about the idiom protects accuracy and relationships. Literalism and silent omission both distort what was meant.
consequencePreviews: A literal translation without context creates an unnecessary conflict.
Here, you flag the ambiguity, explain the intended meaning and check with the speaker.
You may notice that omitting content without saying so distorts the communication.

quests.persona: a mediator between two employees
quests.scene: You're mediating between two employees, Ana and Ben, after a shouting match. Ana says, 'He's always undermining me.' Ben says, 'She never listens.' Both are looking at you for a ruling.
options: I'm not here to decide who's right. I'd like each of you to describe one specific incident, without 'always' or 'never', and say what you'd want to be different. Ana, would you start?

It sounds like you're both to blame. Let's just shake hands and move on, looking back, it wasn't a fully considered answer, so it's worth double-checking — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.

Ana, Ben's complaint sounds fair. You might try listening more, to be fair, that was more of a first reaction, but I'm not totally set on it — and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.
quests.hint: As a mediator, avoid rulings; ask for specific incidents and desired changes.
quests.explanation: Specifics turn accusations into problems that can be solved. Forcing an early truce leaves grievances, and taking sides destroys trust.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you stay neutral, shift from generalisations to specifics and structure the turns.
As a result, a quick fix ignores the underlying issues and both will feel unheard.
As a result, siding with one person ends your neutrality and the mediation.

quests.persona: a doctor and a patient who refuses treatment
quests.scene: You're a doctor. A patient with high blood pressure refuses medication, saying, 'I don't want to be dependent on pills.' You respect his autonomy, but the risk is real, and he has a family history of stroke.
options: I hear you don't want to depend on pills, and that's a reasonable concern. What worries you most about them? Let's talk about the risk to you, and whether lifestyle changes with regular checks could be a first step, so you stay in control of the decisions.
You need to take them. If you don't, you could die of a stroke.

It's your choice. If you don't want to take them, I won't press you, honestly, I hadn't weighed all the details, so take it with a grain of salt — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet, and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.
quests.hint: With a resistant patient, explore the concern, share the risk plainly and offer a stepwise option.
quests.explanation: Understanding his fear opens the door to a compromise. Scare tactics cause defensiveness, and withdrawing abandons him with the risk.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, you respect his view, explore the concern, explain the risk and offer a middle path that keeps his autonomy.
Realistically, fear-based pressure may increase resistance and ends the conversation.
You may notice that deferring completely fails to give him the information and options he needs.

quests.persona: a team of volunteers and a leader who wants to quit
quests.scene: Your best volunteer leader tells you she's exhausted and wants to resign. Losing her would disrupt a big event next month. She's been giving far too much, and you know it.
options: Please don't leave. We'd be lost without you, and the event will collapse, to be honest, it wasn't a fully considered answer, so let me know if that's off — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.

Thank you for telling me, and for everything you've given. I don't want you to burn out. What would make it manageable, fewer tasks, a co-lead or a break after the event? Whatever you decide, I'll support it.

Of course, I understand. I'll find someone else to run the event, admittedly, I hadn't fully worked out how it'd play out, though I'd want to think it over more — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet, and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.
quests.hint: When someone wants to quit from exhaustion, thank them, explore what would make it sustainable and promise support.
quests.explanation: She needs to feel valued and relieved, not guilty. Offering specific adjustments may keep her, and either way she is treated well. Pleading and instant acceptance both miss that.
consequencePreviews: You may notice that guilt-tripping adds to her stress and risks her leaving anyway.
Realistically, you value her, protect her wellbeing and open options without guilt or pressure.
Realistically, accepting immediately without exploring options may lose a willing helper and add to your problems.

quests.persona: a diplomat at a summit
quests.scene: At an international summit, your counterpart says, in front of others, 'Your country's policy is the main obstacle to progress.' Your instructions are to keep talks going and not concede anything publicly.
options: That's an unfair accusation, and your own country's record is much worse, looking back, I hadn't really thought it through, so it's worth double-checking — and a lot depends on details I haven't really looked into yet.
You may be right. We'll consider changing our policy.
I appreciate your frankness. We see it differently, but we share the goal of progress. Perhaps we could discuss specifics in our working session, where we can look at what each side needs.
quests.hint: Under public criticism, stay composed, acknowledge the difference, restate shared goals and move detail to a private setting.
quests.explanation: Composure keeps the talks alive. Counterattacks create a public fight, and concessions breach your mandate.
consequencePreviews: As a result, a public counterattack escalates and blocks the talks.
Realistically, conceding publicly exceeds your instructions and weakens your position.
As a result, you stay composed, note the disagreement, restate the shared goal and move to a private forum.

quests.persona: an elderly relative and a scam caller
quests.scene: Your grandmother tells you proudly that she's about to send $3,000 to a 'grandson in trouble' who phoned her, because he asked her not to tell anyone. She's already at the bank, and calls you as she's about to transfer.
options: Gran, that's a scam. You are being silly. Just don't send anything, in fairness, I was going more on instinct than anything, so feel free to push back — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
Gran, please stop for a minute, before you send anything. I'm not sure it's him. Could you hang up and call his real number? I'll ring him too, and I'll stay on the line with you until we know.

Okay, but keep the receipt so we can check later if it was real, thinking about it now, it wasn't a fully considered answer, so take it with a grain of salt — and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it.
quests.hint: With a possible scam involving someone vulnerable, pause the action, verify independently and stay with them.
quests.explanation: Speed matters, so pause the transfer, and keep her dignity intact. Insults make her resist, and waiting until later is too late.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, calling her silly may make her defensive and less likely to listen.
Here, you act fast, gently, and give a specific verification step while staying with her.
You may notice that letting the transfer go ahead loses money that is hard to recover.

quests.persona: a landlord who wants to sell
quests.scene: Your landlord tells you he's selling the flat and asks you to allow viewings 'whenever convenient for the buyers'. You work from home and have a baby. Your contract allows viewings with 24 hours' notice.
options: I'm happy to cooperate. The lease says twenty-four hours' notice, so could we agree fixed slots, say Tuesday and Thursday afternoons? That gives you regular viewings, and it works with the baby's naps.
No viewings at all. I have a baby and I work from home.
Whenever the buyers like is fine. I'll just fit around them.
quests.hint: When a contract gives you rights, cooperate within them by proposing a workable schedule.
quests.explanation: Fixed slots help both sides and use the notice clause as a basis. Refusing outright is likely to be unreasonable, and unlimited access sacrifices your needs.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, you cooperate, cite your rights lightly and propose a schedule that meets both needs.
You may notice that a flat refusal may breach your obligations and harm the relationship.
As a result, giving up your notice right disrupts your family and work.

quests.persona: a colleague, a rival team and confidential information
quests.scene: During a friendly lunch, a friend from a competing team says, 'Off the record, are you launching the new pricing in March? We need to plan our own.' You are under a confidentiality agreement and you don't want to damage the friendship.
options: I'm not telling you that. It's obviously a trick question, and I don't appreciate it.
Well, I shouldn't say, but you didn't hear it from me: it's probably April.
I can't discuss anything about our plans, as you'd expect me to say the same about yours. Let's talk about something else. How's the new flat?
quests.hint: Refuse confidential requests warmly by noting mutual expectations and changing the subject.
quests.explanation: Treating it as a normal boundary keeps the friendship intact. Accusing is unnecessary, and leaking, even vaguely, breaks your obligation.
consequencePreviews: As a result, the accusation damages the friendship for something that may have been casual.
As a result, hinting breaches your agreement and risks your job.
Here, you set the boundary warmly, without accusing, and steer the conversation.

quests.persona: a negotiation with an ally and an opponent
quests.scene: You're negotiating a contract for your firm. Your counterpart is tough, but your own director keeps interrupting to concede points, weakening your position. The counterpart looks amused.
options: Could we take a five-minute break? I'd like to check something with my colleague, and then we'll come back with our response.
Please let me handle this, sir. You're undermining our position, actually, I hadn't checked how that would actually land, but that could easily change.
Fine, we'll accept those points. I don't want to argue in front of them, honestly, I wasn't considering every angle, so feel free to push back.
quests.hint: When your own side undermines you in a negotiation, call a break rather than arguing in front of the other party.
quests.explanation: A break lets you talk privately and regroup. Public correction reveals disunity, and passive acceptance loses the deal you were working for.
consequencePreviews: You pause the room diplomatically to realign your side without exposing a rift.
Here, correcting your own director in front of the counterpart exposes a weakness.
As a result, going along with the concessions gives away value you meant to protect.

quests.persona: a group of parents, a headteacher and a controversial decision
quests.scene: The headteacher has cut a popular music programme to save money. At the parents' meeting, emotions are high. A parent shouts, 'You don't care about our children!' You're the parent representative and want to be constructive.
options: Yes, exactly! This decision is disgraceful and she should be replaced.

I think we all care about the children, and what we need is a real conversation about the budget. Headteacher, could you show us the figures, and could parents suggest ways to fund a reduced programme?

Let's all calm down. Perhaps we should leave the headteacher to run the school, if I'm being honest, I hadn't checked how that would actually land, so let me know if that's off — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.
quests.hint: In a heated meeting, assume good faith and convert anger into a request for facts and options.
quests.explanation: Data and proposals shift the mood from blame to solutions. Adding to the anger blocks progress, and closing the debate leaves grievances.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, inflaming the room gives the headteacher no way to engage.
Realistically, you de-escalate, assume good faith, and turn the anger into a joint problem-solving task.
Shutting down the discussion ignores parents' legitimate concerns.

quests.persona: a colleague, an employee's honest mistake and the press
quests.scene: A junior colleague accidentally sent private customer data to the wrong email address. A journalist calls you as the press officer and asks, 'Is it true there's been a data breach?' Your legal team is drafting a statement but it isn't ready.
options: There's been no breach. It was just a minor administrative error.
No comment.
We're aware of an incident and are investigating it. We've informed the regulator, and we'll notify affected customers directly. I'll send you a full statement by five today.
quests.hint: In a crisis, confirm what's known, say what is being done and promise a specific time for more.
quests.explanation: Honest facts and a deadline maintain credibility while legal finishes. Minimising is deceptive, and 'no comment' fuels speculation.
consequencePreviews: Minimising an actual breach is misleading and could be exposed later.
Here, silence suggests concealment and leaves the story to others.
As a result, you confirm the essentials truthfully, name the steps taken and commit to a time for the full statement.

quests.persona: your team and a broken promise
quests.scene: Your team worked hard for months on a project, and your director promised bonuses. Now she tells you the budget is frozen and there will be no bonuses this year. She looks upset and asks you to tell the team, because you're their leader.
options: I'll tell them, and I'd like to do it honestly. Could you join me, so that they can hear directly from you why it changed and what, if anything, you can do later? I'd also like to ask you for something we can give them now, such as extra leave.
I can't tell them that. You promised it, so you have to be the one to explain.

Fine, I'll tell them. I'll say it's out of our hands and no one is to blame, admittedly, that was more of a first reaction, so I could be wrong — and honestly the whole situation caught me a bit off guard, and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
quests.hint: When delivering bad news for someone else, share the delivery, be honest about the source and ask for something tangible to offer.
quests.explanation: The team needs the truth from the decision-maker and a sign of good faith. Taking the blame alone misrepresents things, and refusing leaves everyone worse off.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you accept the difficult task, insist on shared accountability and look for a real, immediate gesture.
Realistically, refusing outright may be understandable but breaks your role as leader and damages the relationship.
In this moment, absorbing the message alone leaves you carrying the anger and hides a decision that wasn't yours.

quests.persona: a friend, a family and a difficult honesty
quests.scene: Your best friend proudly shows you the business plan she has spent a year on and asks if you'll co-sign a loan for it. You've spotted serious flaws in her figures. Her family has already invested, and she's emotionally exposed.
options: It looks great. I'm sure it will work, so of course I'll co-sign.

This plan is unrealistic. I won't sign anything, and I'd advise you not to go ahead, if I'm honest, I wasn't considering every angle, though I'd want to think it over more — and honestly the whole situation caught me a bit off guard, and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.

I can see how much this means to you, and I want it to succeed. I'm not comfortable co-signing yet, because I found problems in the sales forecast. Could we go through the numbers together, and maybe get an independent review, before anyone commits more money?
quests.hint: When honesty could hurt, affirm the person, state your specific concern and offer a way to test it together.
quests.explanation: She needs your truth and your support together. Specific concerns plus an independent review is a path forward. Flattery endangers money, and a harsh verdict may cost you the friendship.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, false encouragement puts you and her family at financial risk.
The blunt verdict ignores her feelings and may end both the conversation and the help you could give.
In this moment, you affirm her effort, state your position clearly and propose a constructive route that protects her and her family.

quests.persona: a graduate speaking at an alumni panel
quests.scene: You're invited to speak to students at your old university. In the Q&A, a student asks, 'Honestly, was your degree worth the debt?' Your experience is mixed: it opened doors but the debt has been heavy. The dean, who invited you, is in the room.
options: Absolutely, it was worth every penny, and you should all be very grateful to be here, admittedly, I said that fairly quickly, so let me know if that's off — and there's a decent chance I'd see it differently after sleeping on it, and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.

Honestly, mixed. The degree opened doors I couldn't have opened otherwise, and the debt has limited some choices. What I'd say is, look closely at what you can afford, use the careers service early and talk to people a few years ahead of you about how it worked out.

No, it wasn't. The debt is crushing and universities don't tell you the truth about it, honestly, I wasn't considering every angle, but that could easily change — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything, and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing.
quests.hint: When honesty and the setting pull apart, give a balanced, truthful answer and practical guidance.
quests.explanation: Students deserve an honest, useful answer, and the dean can accept balance. Cheerleading misleads them, and a blanket condemnation isn't accurate either.
consequencePreviews: Here, unqualified praise for the audience's benefit is not honest about your experience.
As a result, you are truthful about both sides, respect the setting and give practical advice.
Here, a one-sided verdict omits the benefits and may be unhelpful to students deciding.
